Jesus talked about the size of faith more than once. When the apostles said, "Increase our faith!" he answered that if they had "faith like a grain of mustard seed," they could say to a mulberry tree, "Be uprooted and planted in the sea," and it would obey (Luke 17:5-6). After the disciples failed with this same boy, he said that faith like a mustard seed could move a mountain (Matthew 17:20). We tend to hear that as "even a little is enough if you can work it up to the right intensity." But the mustard seed was proverbially tiny, and Jesus's point is that the power isn't in the size of the faith. In another parable he describes a mustard seed sown in a field that grows until "the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches" (Matthew 13:32). A seed does nothing sitting on a table. Planted, it grows. The power was never in how much faith you had. It was in what the faith was planted in. So measure your faith not by how much of it you have or how certain it feels, but by what it rests on.

I won't end standing outside this. Many of us don't have the certainty we were raised with, and we aren't getting it back, and some of us have stopped wanting it back, because we've learned it was fragile and a little dishonest. What we can have is smaller and tougher. We believe, and we have unbelief, and we can learn to bring both to Christ the way that father did. On the days we do, the faith holds. Not because we're certain. Because of what it's planted in.

So this study doesn't resolve, and it isn't supposed to. Faith this side of the grave doesn't come with a clean ending, and a study that gave you one would be lying to you. You'll leave with a faith smaller than the one you came in with and, if the work has been truthful, stronger. The questions are still in your hands; you don't have to put them down. But there may be ground under your feet now that wasn't there before, "a tested stone, a precious cornerstone" (Isaiah 28:16). Go carry weight, because that's the only test a faith finally faces: not whether it can win an argument, but whether it can hold a life. And when the unbelief rises again, as it will, do what the father did. Bring it. Say it out loud. "I believe; help my unbelief!"

scriptureStudy.note: "I believe; help my unbelief!" The father confesses faith and doubt in one breath and brings both to Jesus, who answers him. Faith doesn't have to wait until doubt is gone before it comes.
"If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move." The power isn't in the size of the faith but in what it rests on.
"Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen." Faith by definition isn't sight, so a faith with open questions isn't defective. It's doing what the word means.
"For I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me." Not what but whom. A faith that holds rests finally on a person.

"Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." Peter doesn't stay because he has no questions. He stays because he has weighed the alternatives and found nowhere better to put his trust.

"But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning." Hope comes back not by denying the grief that fills the book but by calling one true thing to mind in the middle of it.
"A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench." God isn't impatient with a damaged or flickering faith. He's careful with it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the old phrase "faith seeking understanding," which Anselm of Canterbury used in the eleventh century for the right relationship between believing and questioning. In that tradition faith and hard questions aren't enemies. Faith is where inquiry begins: a trust placed in God that then goes looking to understand what it has trusted, unafraid of questions because the trust doesn't depend on answering them all first.

Set that beside the two failures the last session names: a faith that demands belief without any inquiry and treats every question as a threat, and a reason that won't commit to anything it can't first prove and so never trusts at all. Faith seeking understanding refuses both. You can rest your weight on God while still wrestling with what you don't understand, and the wrestling is a sign of a faith confident enough in its foundation to ask hard things. Consider too the old observation that the opposite of faith may not be doubt so much as indifference, not caring enough to ask. A faith that can hold weight keeps seeking understanding from inside a trust that doesn't depend on the search being finished.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that near the end of a study like this one, a man who has said almost nothing for five weeks finally speaks. He came hoping to get back the faith he grew up with, the one where everything fit and nobody asked hard questions, and he's disappointed, because it hasn't happened and he can tell now it never will.

You might ask him what he has instead. Perhaps he says it's a faith he can't really defend in an argument anymore, one with holes in it, held with his eyes open. He still has no answers about suffering, or the passages that trouble him, or why his prayers for his marriage have gone unanswered for years. But he's noticed something. He has stopped pretending. He's quit performing a certainty he didn't feel, in front of God and everyone, and oddly the unpretending faith feels more solid than the certain one did, because it isn't bracing against the next question. It has already let the questions in and is still standing.

You could point him to the father in Mark 9, who said "I believe" and "help my unbelief" in the same breath, brought both to Jesus, and got his answer. Don't try to wrap it up for him. The man hasn't recovered his old faith. He has something smaller and tougher that no longer requires him to lie, and that may be the best place for the study to end.

leaderPrimer:
Before this group trusts a word you say, it will decide what you are, and the options are narrow. Either you're one more church official sent to manage them back into line, or you're someone who can be told the truth. Every minute of the first session is really about that, and you can't answer it with reassurance. You answer it by not flinching. Someone will name what a pastor did, to them or to someone they love, and the room will watch your face for the reflex: the qualification, the defense of the institution. If it shows, even kindly, the study is over, whatever happens in the weeks after. Say instead what they've rarely heard a leader say: that what was done to them was wrong. And mean it.

Where the story includes abuse, say that leaving was right, that a trauma informed counselor matters more than any session in this guide, and have the name ready. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities. If a child may be at risk, report it to the police.

The hazard under all five weeks is your own discomfort. Watching someone take a faith apart in front of you is frightening, and the fear will push you to hurry them toward any landing so the free fall stops. Don't. The worst decisions about faith are the fast ones, in either direction. Your job isn't to win the room back by week five. It's to slow the sorting down until people can tell what they're actually holding: the gospel, or the bundle it came wrapped in, the politics, the culture, the man who hurt them. Most of them aren't leaving Jesus. They're leaving a version of him somebody sold them, and helping them tell the difference is the whole study.

I don't stand outside this, and you don't either. Pastors like me did the bundling, and pastors have watched people leave over real wounds and called it their unbelief to let ourselves off the hook. Carry your own questions toward God, out loud, where people can see. The last session aims at a faith that can hold weight, smaller than the faith some of them started with and stronger. Don't promise the old certainty back. Promise rock, if they dig, and then dig where they can watch you.

faq.q: Is this study going to try to talk me out of my doubts?
faq.a: No. Its aim is examination instead of leaving by default, so that whatever you decide, you decide about the real thing rather than the bundle of culture, politics and institution the faith came wrapped in. It refuses to defend the version of faith you may be right to leave, and it spends a whole session naming what the church got wrong, including harm done by people like me. If you came braced to be argued back into a position, you'll find a study that takes your questions more seriously than the people who handed you the answers did, and a leader's guide that tells the leader not to rush you.

faq.q: Does this study think doubt is a sin?
faq.a: No, and the second session exists to say so from Scripture. The Bible's doubters are among its heroes: the psalmist asking how long God will hide his face, Job arguing for chapters and being vindicated, John the Baptist asking from prison whether Jesus was the one, Thomas refusing to believe without the wounds. Jude's instruction to the church is "have mercy on those who doubt" (Jude 22). The study does name a corrosive doubt that loves the question more than the truth, but it says the difference isn't whether you doubt. It's which way you carry the doubt, toward God or away.

faq.q: I was hurt by a church. Does this study take that seriously or just tell me to forgive and stay?
faq.a: It takes it with complete seriousness, and the third session is built around it. The study refuses the line "you shouldn't leave over hypocrites" when it's aimed at someone being harmed, because in that case it's the institution protecting itself at the victim's expense. It shows that Jesus didn't counsel patience with religion that crushed people, and that in Ezekiel God says he is against the shepherds who ruled with harshness. Leaving an abusive church isn't leaving God; sometimes it's the only way left to follow him. And it says, more than once, that where abuse is part of your story a trauma informed counselor matters more than any reading plan, and that getting out is the right thing to do. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities.

faq.q: If I just trusted God more, would the doubts go away?
faq.a: Not necessarily, and the study won't promise that. Where questioning is really a heart looking for permission to leave something already abandoned, trust does address it. But much doubt isn't that. It's a response to a real contradiction, a real wound, a real question nobody would answer, and telling that doubt to trust harder only stacks shame on top. The Bible's doubters weren't short on faith, and Jesus met them with evidence and presence rather than rebuke. Some doubt is settled by trust. Some is settled only slowly, by careful examination and sometimes by years.

faq.q: What's the difference between deconstruction and just losing your faith?
faq.a: That difference is what the first session is about. Most people taking their faith apart aren't leaving Jesus; they're leaving a version of him somebody sold them. The faith came as one bundle, doctrine, institution, people and God, taped together and handed over as if it were all one thing, so when it comes apart everything seems to fall at once. The work is sorting, not burning: looking at each piece to see what it is, keeping what's true and letting go of what was only wrapping. From the outside, losing your faith and sifting it can look the same. The difference is whether you ever separated the real thing from everything it came bundled with.

faq.q: Is the goal of the study to get me to rebuild and stay a Christian?
faq.a: The goal is to help you decide truthfully about the real thing, not to engineer an outcome. The study won't rush you to rebuild; demolition takes the time it takes. But it does name a danger the deconstruction conversation rarely admits: tearing down can become a permanent identity, a new certainty built on being right about everyone who hasn't seen through it, the same ground as the fundamentalism it replaced. So the study turns, eventually and gently, toward building, on whatever has actually survived your questions, even if it's much smaller than what you started with, and even if for now you're still looking.

faq.q: What if, after all this, I conclude it isn't true?
faq.a: Then that's your conclusion, and the study has refused from the start to talk you out of it, because a faith you were argued back into would be as borrowed as the one you inherited. The fourth session faces this directly. It asks only that the conclusion be reached carefully rather than by default, about the real thing rather than the bundle, and it points out that "the rubble is just the truth" is itself a foundation you'd be building a life on. The study's request isn't that you land on faith. It's that you decide slowly, with company, rather than fast and alone.

faq.q: I've been doubting for years and haven't landed anywhere. Is something wrong with me?
faq.a: No. There's no deadline, and nobody is timing you or waiting at the last session with an altar call. You're allowed to take years, and many people who eventually rebuilt something true did just that. The pressure to land quickly, in either direction, is the same pressure that often broke trust in the first place. The study does distinguish "not ready yet," which is fine and may last a long while, from a settled refusal ever to decide, but it never treats the time itself as failure.

faq.q: Why does the study keep turning the questions back on the writer and the leader instead of just helping the doubters?
faq.a: Because you can't help a doubting person from above without the help turning into either shame or distance. I'm a pastor, and pastors like me did the bundling, taping God and politics and institution together and handing it over as one package. We've watched people leave over wounds the church gave them and called it their unbelief. So I've tried to write from inside the wrestling, and the study asks every leader to do the same. A leader who can say "I have questions too, and I've been part of the problem" can sit beside someone who is deconstructing rather than over them.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Is this just a clever way to keep believers from leaving?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion. The study tries to earn an answer by refusing the cheap version of exactly that. It doesn't defend the indefensible; it spends a whole session naming the church's real harm, including abuse and cover-up. It takes the strongest objections seriously instead of knocking down straw men, and it says plainly that if careful examination ends in the conclusion that it isn't true, that conclusion should be reached and not dodged. What it asks isn't that you stay, but that you decide about the real thing rather than the cultural bundle, and that you weigh the best case for faith alongside the best case against it.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have serious doubts myself?
faq.a: Your doubts aren't a disqualification. They may be your best qualification. The study is meant to be led by a fellow traveler, not by someone who has conquered every question. Every discussion question carries a note for you, and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising. Being truthful about your own questions may be the most pastoral thing in the room. What you do need is to refuse to shame anyone, to keep the group safe for the wounded and the questioning, to point anyone who has been abused toward real help without judgment, and to keep Christ above both recovered certainty and permanent exile in your own heart.

faq.q: Does the study promise that if I follow it my faith will be restored?
faq.a: No. It ends without resolution on purpose, because faith this side of the grave doesn't come with a clean ending, and a study that promised one would be lying to you. The aim isn't a faith that has answered every question but a faith that can hold weight, smaller than the one you started with and, if the work has been truthful, stronger. For some the rebuilding will come soon, for some it will take years, and for some the conclusion will surprise them. What the study offers is a way to take the questions apart in the open, with company, toward the one who meets doubters with mercy and "a bruised reed he will not break" (Isaiah 42:3).

timeline.event: The Psalms give Israel words for doubt that take the questions straight to God, asking how long he will hide his face, so that Scripture supplies language for wrestling and not only against it.
The book of Job, whose date scholars still debate, vindicates the man who argued with God over the friends who defended God with tidy answers.

Isaiah condemns a religion that honors God with the lips while the heart is far away, whose fear of God is "a commandment taught by men," drawing a line between God and the traditions wrapped around him.
Jesus drives the money-changers from the temple and calls the religious leaders whitewashed tombs, aiming his fiercest words at religious authority that crushed the vulnerable.
The Jerusalem council rules that Gentile believers need not take on circumcision and the food laws, the church's first formal decision that the cultural wrapping isn't the gospel itself (Acts 15).
Augustine writes his Confessions, recording his long road from unbelief through real intellectual struggle into faith.
Anselm of Canterbury describes faith seeking understanding, treating believing and questioning as partners rather than enemies.

Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses begin the Reformation, in which people who loved the church tried to sift the gospel from centuries of accumulated practice and refused to defend what they saw as corruption.
The final Latin edition of John Calvin's Institutes sets out the distinction between the visible church, always mixed with hypocrisy, and the church known to God alone.
Søren Kierkegaard publishes his attack on a Christendom in which everyone was Christian by birth, pressing for a personal, examined faith.
C. S. Lewis, who came to faith from atheism, publishes Mere Christianity, drawn from his wartime radio talks, taking the skeptic's questions seriously.
The word "deconstruction" comes into wide use for examining an inherited faith, often after exposed church abuse or the fusing of faith with party politics.
A wider reckoning with documented church abuse and cover-up, and many younger people leaving churches, presses the church to tell faithful sifting from abandonment and to take its own harm seriously.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for coming. It takes courage to talk about taking your faith apart in a room full of people. Three things before we start. First, this is a safe room. You can say "I don't know if I believe any of this anymore" here. You can name what a church or a person did to you, and nobody is going to defend them or rush to fix you. Second, this study takes your questions seriously, all of them, and it will never tell you that doubting is a sin or that leaving a place that harmed you is leaving God. We'll see that from the Bible itself, which is full of doubters who weren't its villains. Third, I'm in this with you. Pastors and church leaders did a lot of the bundling, taping God and politics and institution together and handing it over as one thing. I have questions too. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it closer, into the questions you carry at night and the decisions nobody else sees you make, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though it isn't settled, because deconstruction doesn't settle on a schedule and pretending it does would be a lie. Take your questions toward Jesus this week rather than carrying them alone or settling them fast in private. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions. And if something in tonight tells you that what was done to you was abuse and you need a counselor, please hear that as wisdom and not as a failure of faith, because leaving a place that harmed you is the right thing to do. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for being here.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and shame, and take session 1's opening questions slowly. Say plainly that doubt isn't a sin and that nobody is being timed.
Week 2: Session 1, What You Are Actually Taking Apart, full discussion and the sorting practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Is Doubt a Sin, with extra time on the Bible's doubters and the difference between seeking doubt and corrosive doubt.
Week 4: Session 3, When the Church Is the Reason, taken slowly and gently, with help resources ready for anyone carrying abuse.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: the difference between an imperfect church and an abusive one, with room for the letter practice and for grief.
Week 6: Session 4, Rebuilding on Rock, Not on Demolition.
Week 7: Session 5, A Faith That Can Hold Weight.
Week 8: Looking back. Revisit the creeds and lists, the Scripture index, and what each person is carrying toward Christ, with room for anyone still deciding slowly.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, what you're taking apart and whether doubt is a sin.
Week 2: Session 3, When the Church Is the Reason, with extra time on church harm and the help resources. Never rushed.
Week 3: Session 4, Rebuilding on Rock, Not on Demolition.
Week 4: Session 5, A Faith That Can Hold Weight, with a short time of looking back at the end.

A Church Called Tov, Scot McKnight and Laura Barringer, for anyone trying to picture a healthy church culture against the one that harmed them.
The Sin of Certainty, Peter Enns, for those wrestling with the difference between faith and certainty, read alongside the study's own handling of it.

Confessions, Augustine of Hippo, for anyone who wants to walk with a mind that worked through long doubt into a faith that held.

glossary.definition: Examining an inherited faith piece by piece to see what's actually true. The study treats it not as betrayal or fad but as what a thinking person does when the answers they were given stop carrying weight, and it distinguishes faithful sifting from abandonment.

The single package in which most people receive their faith, doctrine, institution, people and God taped together as if they were one thing, so that pulling on any thread feels like losing all of it. The first work is untying it.

The cultural, political and institutional additions wrapped around the gospel and handed over as if they were the gospel. Much of it deserves to fall; the study distinguishes it from the load-bearing faith underneath.
Doubt that asks because it wants to know, and carries its questions toward God rather than away from him, like the psalmist, Job, John the Baptist and Thomas.

Doubt that loves the question more than the truth and refuses every answer, making inquiry a permanent address instead of a road. It differs from seeking doubt not in whether it exists but in which way it's carried.

Using religious authority, Scripture or community to control, silence or harm, especially when an institution protects the powerful and abandons the wounded. The study refuses to defend it and treats leaving an abusive church as faithful.

glossary.term: The visible church and the church known to God
glossary.definition: The distinction between the institution as it actually exists, always mixed with hypocrisy and sometimes captured by corrupt people, and the whole body of those who truly belong to Christ, known finally to God alone. Leaving a corrupt institution isn't the same as leaving the body of Christ.
What a faith finally rests on, which the storm shows when fair weather has hidden it. Following Jesus's story of the two builders, the study measures a rebuilt faith by whether its foundation holds.
Jesus's image for a faith whose power isn't in its size but in what it's planted in. A small rooted faith outlasts a large faith built on sand.
Anselm's phrase for believing and questioning as partners, a trust in God that then goes looking to understand what it has trusted, unafraid of the questions.
Demanding belief without inquiry and treating every question as a threat. One of two failures the study warns against; the other is refusing ever to trust.

glossary.term: A faith that can hold weight
glossary.definition: The study's aim, a faith not certain of every answer but rooted enough to carry the real load of a life, smaller than the inherited one and stronger, like the father who said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Deconstruction usually gets handled two wrong ways in church, panicked over as betrayal or celebrated as enlightenment, and few people do the real work of telling the gospel from the baggage it came wrapped in. This five-session study looks at what you're actually taking apart, whether doubt is a sin, the wounds the church itself causes, rebuilding on rock rather than rubble, and a faith small enough to be true and strong enough to hold weight. It takes your questions seriously, refuses to defend what the church got wrong, and never shames anyone for doubting. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are, not finished.

quoteCards: Deconstruction isn't betrayal and it isn't a fad. It's what a thinking person does when the answers they were handed stop carrying weight.
Many people aren't leaving Jesus. They're leaving a version of him somebody sold them.
The Bible is full of doubters, and they aren't its villains. What matters is which way you carry the doubt.
Jesus didn't counsel patience with religion that crushed people. He overturned the tables.
Leaving a church that harmed you isn't leaving God. Sometimes it's the only way left to follow him.
Demolition isn't a foundation. You can't live in the rubble forever, and you were never meant to.
A small true thing built on rock will outlast a large impressive thing built on sand.
The father said, "I believe; help my unbelief!" That's a faith that can hold weight.
